data.title: Singapore's energy ministry says piped gas supply from Indonesia is fully restored
data.description:
Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said on Friday that Indonesia had fully restored its piped natural gas supply to the city-state on November 12.

  • A ministry spokesperson added that there had been "no further notification of supply reduction"

  • Indonesia had earlier cut 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day (mmscfd) from its piped natural ​gas exports to Singapore in October, diverting supply ‌to its domestic power sector

  • Singapore's Energy Market Authority said at the time that the total reduction ⁠amounted to 17 billion British thermal units per day (bbtud) over a period of 18 days, which is "less ​than 2% of our total daily gas demand of more than 1,000 ​bbtud"

  • Indonesia's energy ministry and upstream regulator did not immediately respond to a request for comment

data.title: German Recovery Gathers Pace But Lacks Private Investment — Market Talk
data.description: Germany's economy is showing signs of recovery after three years of stagnation, expanding 1% in the first three quarters of 2026, analysts at Berenberg say in a note. Fiscal stimulus, stronger exports and a weaker euro have helped offset high energy costs, while improving sentiment points to further growth as energy prices ease next year. The government's spending package is already boosting public investment, particularly in defense, and growth could accelerate to 1.6% in 2028, they say. But the recovery remains uneven. "Private investment has declined since 2019," the analysts say, highlighting the need for deeper supply-side reforms. Improving conditions for businesses will require progress on pension, healthcare and elderly-care reforms to revive private investment and deliver a more sustainable economic recovery. (don.forbes@wsj.com)

data.title: Top UN Court Finds Myanmar Guilty Of Genocide Against Rohingya
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during military operations in Rakhine State in the last decade. It is the first time the UN's top court has found a state responsible for genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

At the end of a three-hour ruling at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, President Yuji Iwasawa also declared that Myanmar had failed to prevent and punish genocide, after detailing how the eastern Asian country's military had perpetrated 'extreme violence' against mainly Muslim Rohingya communities in Rakhine state.

The ruling establishes that Myanmar's security forces and other State organs intentionally committed specifically prohibited acts covered by Article II of the Genocide Convention.

The ICJ ruling came after studying graphic evidence and testimonies provided by survivors and reports from international investigators describing how Rohingya villages and bridges had been set alight and bulldozed, with men and boys executed and girls and women raped during military clearance operations in northern Rakhine in 2017.

The military clearance operations also involved the murder of infants, which 'supports the inference that Myanmar's security forces acted with the intent to prevent births among the group,' Judge Iwasawa added.

Delivering the court's ruling, the ICJ President described how the mainly Muslim Rohingya living in Rakhine state in western Myanmar had been the target of successive clearance operations by the State military, after decades of intercommunal violence.

The 2017 clearance operations prompted widespread international condemnation after some 700,000 Rohingya fled northern Rakhine state across the border to Bangladesh.

According to the court, an estimated 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the clearance operations, citing supporting evidence.

A separate study estimated that the military and the local Rakhine population killed at least 25,000 Rohingya people.

The case at the ICJ was initiated by The Gambia in November 2019. It has become one of the most closely watched proceedings before the world's highest court.

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority in western Myanmar's Rakhine State, were stripped of citizenship under the 1982 Citizenship Law and have faced decades of state discrimination, movement restrictions, and abuse.

More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh during the 2017 crisis, adding to roughly one million Rohingya refugees living in Bangladeshi camps.

Since 2024, fighting in Rakhine State involving Myanmar's military and the Arakan Army has continued to endanger Rohingya civilians.

The court heard that nearly 400 villages - approximately 40 per cent of the almost 1,000 villages in the three townships of northern Rakhine state - were partially or totally destroyed during and after the 2017 clearance operations.

Myanmar's authorities have consistently denied committing genocide, arguing that military 'clearance operations' were counterterrorism actions responding to attacks by armed groups such as the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The ICJ rejected that defense, finding that the military failed to distinguish between militants and civilians

The Court ordered the government of Myanmar to enact legislation giving full effect to its obligations under the Genocide Convention; to take immediate steps to investigate all persons suspected of having committed acts contrary to the Convention and, if warranted, to prosecute and punish them.

In addition, the ruling orders Myanmar to provide guarantee that such violence is not repeated in the future.

Finally, the Court decided that Myanmar should transmit to it within two years a report on the measures of restitution it has adopted and the amount and modalities of compensation.

The judgment is binding on the parties to the case and without appeal.

UN leadership, human rights organizations, and several governments welcomed the judgment as a milestone for accountability.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed the judgment as a 'powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide. It is a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand.'

data.title: Asia spot prices fall to 6-week low on weak demand, improved supplies
data.description:
By Emily Chow

Asia spot liquefied natural gas prices slipped for a third consecutive week, weighed down by weaker demand and comfortable inventories in Asia, and improved supplies from the Strait of Hormuz and the US.

The average price for January delivery into northeast Asia (LNG-AS) was estimated at $26.90 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) this week, down from $31.30/mmBtu the previous week and the lowest since October 9.

Continued LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz and comfortable Asian inventories that limit spot buying interest are easing market pressures, said Ole Dramdal, senior analyst at Rystad Energy.

Some buying interest, however, was visible in South and Southeast Asia, he said, with Thailand, Pakistan and Vietnam showing buying interest.

In northeast Asia, buyers have stepped back from the spot market, with Chinese firms purchasing only enough to meet storage targets, South Korean buyers already covered for winter, and Japanese demand well supplied by long-term contracts, said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus.

"And at least four cargoes have diverted away from Egypt this week, prompting further immediate supply availability," he added.

"Egyptian demand has fallen as the nation has cut some fertiliser and industrial supply, and has increased fuel oil imports to replace some gas in power generation."

In Europe, S&P Global Commodity Insights assessed its daily Northwest Europe LNG price benchmark for cargoes delivered in December on an ex-ship basis at $26.765/mmBtu on Thursday, a discount of $0.53/mmBtu to the price at the Dutch TTF gas hub.

Spark Commodities assessed it at $26.572/mmBtu, while Argus assessed the January price at $26.65/mmBtu.

"European LNG prices declined sharply over the week as improving global supply expectations and weak Asian competition outweighed tightening European winter fundamentals," said Aly Blakeway, head of Atlantic LNG at S&P Global Energy, adding that US feedgas around record-high levels pointed to strong Atlantic Basin export availability.

"Middle Eastern supply also continued its gradual recovery. Qatar and Abu Dhabi exported around a cargo per day during the first half of November."

European gas markets, however, remain tight heading into year-end, with low storage levels leaving limited room to absorb additional shocks, said Hans van Cleef, head of energy research at EqoLibrium.

"Weather is the main short-term swing factor; an early cold spell would accelerate withdrawals and create chaos. The issues around the Strait of Hormuz remains the key geopolitical supply risk."

In LNG freight, Atlantic rates fell to $20,500 a day, while Pacific rates declined to $52,000 a day, said Spark Commodities analyst Qasim Afghan.

The US front-month arbitrage to northeast Asia via the Cape of Good Hope continues to point firmly to Europe, while the Nigerian prompt arbitrage, also via the Cape, is pointing to Europe for a fourth straight week, he added.

data.title: Bitcoin, Ether Edge Higher But Stay Near Multimonth Lows
data.description:
By Joe Stonor

Major cryptocurrencies edged higher Friday but failed to recover sharp losses from the last session as investors ditched risky assets.

Bitcoin was up 0.1% at $61,559 in early European trade, its lowest level since early July. Ether also rose but failed to significantly regain losses, adding 0.2% to $1,743.

Bitcoin fell sharply Thursday to trade close to $61,500, as Anthropic's IPO failed to spark a broader stock market rally. The cryptocurrency trades around 29% lower than its September peak.

Increased institutional adoption of digital assets is proving a near-term headwind for crypto assets, rather than a boon, said Nidal Abdel Hadi, chief executive of investment group Finoro. Higher correlation to stocks makes crypto more vulnerable to broader risk-off sentiment shifts.

"The provocative possibility is that bitcoin's integration into mainstream finance has weakened its ability to behave independently of traditional liquidity cycles," Hadi said.

For the day ahead, U.S. consumer sentiment data will help shape inflation expectations and, in turn, Federal Reserve policy. Expectations for increased Fed tightening are bearish for nonyielding digital assets.

Write to Joe Stonor at josephmichael.stonor@wsj.com

data.title: INTERVIEW - European solar manufacturing needs stronger EU support, HoloSolis CEO says
data.description:
November 20 (Renewables Now) - French solar manufacturer HoloSolis is targeting the start of production at its planned 5-GW gigafactory in Hambach by late 2029 or early 2030, with its next fundraising round dependent on the adoption of sufficiently ambitious EU legislation to support European-made photovoltaic products.

In an interview with Renewables Now, the company's new CEO, Henri Poupart-Lafarge, discusses the project's financing and revised timeline, its strategy to build a European supply chain and the challenges of competing with established Asian manufacturers.

What is the current status of the Hambach gigafactory project and what are the remaining milestones before construction can begin?

HoloSolis has just closed its first fundraising round, securing EUR 15 million (USD 16.5m), and has been granted around EUR 400 million in public financing from both France and the EU.

The remaining milestones are to complete the detailed engineering (made possible by the EUR-15-million fundraising round), conclude the relevant grant agreements, advance the next financing steps, and complete procurement and construction preparations.

Previous statements indicated that construction would begin in 2027, with the first panels expected in 2028. Are these still your targets?

Before being able to finalise the next fundraising round, we need strong and ambitious regulation at the EU level through the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). This legislation is expected to be finalised next year. We will then be able to start fundraising for the construction of the first building by mid-2027. Construction will start in mid-2028, and production will begin at the end of 2029 or in early 2030.

Have you already secured agreements with potential customers for the factory’s future output?

We have secured letters of intent from customers covering more than 30 GW of production, representing strong commercial interest in the project. However, firm contracts will only be signed after the publication of the IAA, provided that the legislation is strong enough to recognise the value of European-made cells and modules.

How dependent will the gigafactory be on imported components and raw materials?

Our objective is to build a genuinely European industrial base for cells and modules, while being realistic about the current structure of global supply chains. Some upstream materials, specialised equipment and components will initially need to be sourced internationally because European capacity is not yet available at the required scale.

Our priority is to reduce strategic dependency through European sourcing wherever possible. Europe still benefits from companies involved in silicon extraction, such as Ferroglobe, and refining, such as Wacker Chemie. Start-ups are also emerging to bring the entire supply chain back to Europe: ReSilicon for silicon refining, and Sunwafe for ingots and wafers. We hope to offer fully EU-made modules as soon as possible.

What would you consider a healthy balance between domestic European solar manufacturing and imports from China?

A healthy balance would mean that Europe has sufficient domestic production to protect its strategic interests, maintain industrial know-how and support deployment in times of geopolitical or supply-chain disruption. Imports can remain part of the market, but they should complement European production rather than replace it.

The EU’s objective of having at least 40% of deployed PV made in Europe provides a useful benchmark.

Complete decoupling from China is not realistic in the short term, particularly given China's dominance in polysilicon and upstream manufacturing. Europe must start by protecting a share of the PV market, even if it is small at first, to allow manufacturing to be reshored.

What would need to happen in the European market for you to commit to a second production line or another gigafactory?

We would need two conditions: a strong IAA that creates a dedicated market for European-made PV components, and visibility on this addressable market. A second production line or factory would be considered once the Hambach plant is financed, operational and demonstrating that European manufacturing can compete at scale.

Have you already identified potential locations for additional manufacturing facilities, either in France or elsewhere in Europe?

Our immediate priority is to deliver the Hambach project. Any decision on a new plant will depend on market demand, public policy, infrastructure, financing and the performance of the first factory.

If European-made solar panels remain more expensive than imported alternatives, who should ultimately pay the difference?

The IAA focuses on two main market segments: public procurement and national auctions. Many PV projects are being developed with government support. The main aim is to channel this funding towards projects that use European-made panels.

It will be more expensive at first. Governments should provide targeted and temporary support to correct the structural disadvantages created by subsidies, dumping and externalities in international markets. However, there will also be some rewards, mainly through the creation of local jobs and additional tax revenues for governments.

The additional cost will be relatively low, however, as PV modules account for only 10% to 15% of a project's CAPEX. The impact of using European-made PV panels will be lower than that of the increase in financing costs we have seen in recent months.

What will be your main priorities during your first 12 months as CEO?

My priorities will be closely connected. First, securing strong and protective European regulation to create a market for our products. Second, finalising the industrial design, technology partnerships and supply chain. Third, converting customer interest into bankable commercial agreements. Finally, preparing the next fundraising round for the construction of the first buildings.

(EUR 1.0 = USD 1.099)

data.title: Anthropic shares fall 6% in pre-market trading after blockbuster debut amid global selloff over AI fears
data.description:
Shares of Anthropic, the maker of Claude AI, fell more than 6 percent in pre-market trading on November 20, giving back a part of the gains made during its blockbuster Wall Street debut a day earlier.

Anthropic shares were trading at $91 apiece, down 6.35 percent, as of 2:50 pm IST on November 20. The stock had closed its first trading session on the Nasdaq at $97.17 on Thursday, November 19, after surging 17.07 percent from its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The decline came amid concerns over intensifying competition in the artificial intelligence (AI) market after reports emerged that Apple was developing its own autonomous AI agent. The move could put Apple in more direct competition with AI developers such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms in the rapidly expanding market for autonomous AI tools.

The weakness in Anthropic shares also came against the backdrop of a broad sell-off in US equities. On Thursday, all three major US stock indices ended sharply lower, with technology and AI-linked stocks facing considerable selling pressure.

Despite the latest decline, Anthropic shares were still trading around 9.6 percent above their IPO price, indicating that the stock had retained most of its listing-day gains.

Anthropic made history on November 19 by raising approximately $81.34 billion through its IPO, making it the largest stock market debut on record and surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX.

The company priced its shares at $83 apiece, above the initially indicated price range of $70-$78. Its shares opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, marking a premium of around 34 percent over the IPO price.
